documents.overview: A process is an active execution of a program with its own memory and state, managed by the operating system through a process control block. Processes go through states like new, ready, running, waiting, and terminated, and switching between them involves context switches that temporarily halt user work. Unix creates processes via fork and exec, using copy-on-write for efficiency, while threads allow shared memory and faster execution within a process. Threads can be user-level or kernel-level, with different trade-offs in speed and scheduling flexibility. Processes communicate through mechanisms like pipes, shared memory, message queues, and signals.

key_points.text: A process is an active program in execution with its own memory and state, including separate text, data, heap, and stack segments.
The operating system maintains a process control block for each process, storing details like registers, program counter, scheduling info, memory mappings, open files, and CPU usage.
Processes cycle through states: new, ready, running, waiting (blocked), and terminated, with transitions triggered by completion, I/O, or time slices.
A context switch saves and restores process state, causing overhead and cache misses as the CPU switches between processes.
Unix creates processes in two steps: fork duplicates the parent process (using copy-on-write for efficiency), and exec replaces the child’s program.
A child process’s exit status remains in the process table as a zombie until the parent calls wait, and orphaned children are adopted by init.
Threads are lightweight execution units within a process that share memory but have their own stack and registers, enabling parallelism and responsiveness.

documents.overview: CPU scheduling decides which ready process runs next on limited CPU cores, balancing trade-offs like utilization, throughput, and response time. Schedulers can be preemptive or non-preemptive, with modern systems favoring preemption to prevent runaway processes. Common policies include first-come, first-served, shortest job first, round robin, and priority-based approaches, each with strengths and weaknesses. Multicore systems also require managing process placement to minimize cache misses and balance load.

key_points.text: The short-term scheduler selects which ready process runs next, handling context switches and dispatch latency to manage CPU allocation.
Key scheduling metrics include CPU utilization, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time, and response time, with priorities depending on whether the system is batch or interactive.
Preemptive scheduling interrupts a running process to allocate the CPU to another, preventing a single long-running process from monopolizing resources.
First-come, first-served scheduling runs processes in arrival order but can cause long waits for short jobs due to the convoy effect, leaving I/O devices idle.
Shortest job first minimizes average waiting time by prioritizing the shortest predicted CPU burst, but requires estimating burst lengths and risks starvation for long jobs.
Round robin assigns fixed time quanta to processes, improving response time for interactive work but requiring careful quantum selection to avoid excessive context switching.
Priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes, so aging gradually increases priorities over time to ensure fairness.

documents.overview: Synchronization in concurrent programming prevents race conditions by managing access to shared data. It relies on hardware-supported atomic instructions and various locking mechanisms like spinlocks, mutexes, and semaphores. These tools solve classic problems such as the critical section, bounded-buffer, and readers-writers problems while addressing challenges like priority inversion. Advanced techniques like monitors, condition variables, and lock-free designs further refine control over thread coordination.

key_points.text: Race conditions occur when threads share data and the outcome depends on the timing of their operations, such as lost increments in a shared counter.
A critical section is code that accesses shared data and must be executed by only one thread at a time. Correct solutions require mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting.
Hardware provides atomic instructions like test-and-set and compare-and-swap to safely implement locks without relying on program-order guarantees.

Spinlocks use atomic instructions to repeatedly check a lock until it becomes available, wasting CPU time but avoiding sleep overhead. They are suitable for short critical sections in single-core or interrupt contexts.

Mutexes allow only one thread to access a critical section at a time, putting blocked threads to sleep on a waiting list and waking one when the lock is released. They require the acquiring thread to release the lock.

Semaphores are counters with atomic wait (P) and signal (V) operations. Binary semaphores act like locks, while counting semaphores limit access to a pool of resources. Unlike mutexes, semaphores have no owner and allow any thread to signal.
The bounded-buffer problem uses three semaphores—a mutex, an empty counter, and a full counter—to coordinate producers and consumers without deadlock, requiring careful ordering of operations.

documents.overview: A deadlock occurs when threads are stuck waiting for each other’s resources, preventing progress. It requires four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Strategies to handle deadlock include prevention (eliminating one condition), avoidance (granting requests only if the system remains safe), detection and recovery (identifying and resolving deadlocks after they occur), or ignoring them (the ostrich approach). Other issues like starvation and livelock differ from deadlock but can cause similar problems.

key_points.text: A deadlock happens when threads are blocked in a cycle of waiting for each other’s resources, halting progress without corrupting data.
Four conditions must hold simultaneously for a deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Removing any one prevents deadlock.
Deadlocks can be visualized using a resource-allocation graph, where cycles indicate deadlocks for single-instance resources. Multiple instances of a resource complicate detection.
Prevention strategies break one of the four conditions, such as enforcing a global lock order to prevent circular wait or requiring all resources to be requested at once.
Avoidance, like Dijkstra’s banker’s algorithm, grants requests only if the system remains in a safe state where all threads can eventually finish.
Detection involves periodically scanning for cycles in wait-for graphs, while recovery may involve aborting threads, preempting resources, or rolling back changes.
Some systems, like Linux and Windows, avoid handling deadlocks in application threads, relying on programmers to prevent them (the ostrich approach).

documents.overview: Memory management ensures multiple programs share physical memory safely by using virtual address spaces and hardware-based translation. The system uses techniques like segmentation and paging to manage memory efficiently, avoiding fragmentation and enabling protection and sharing. Hardware components like the TLB speed up address translation, while multi-level page tables reduce overhead for large address spaces. The kernel manages its own memory separately to maintain security and performance, though recent vulnerabilities have required additional safeguards.

key_points.text: Virtual address spaces allow multiple processes to share physical memory without interfering with each other. Each process sees a continuous range of addresses starting at zero, while the hardware translates these into physical addresses.

The base and limit registers provide a simple translation scheme where the base register holds the starting physical address of a process, and the limit register defines its size. This method requires a contiguous block of physical memory per process.

External fragmentation occurs when free memory becomes scattered into small holes due to variable-sized allocations, while internal fragmentation wastes space inside fixed-size allocations. Compaction can reduce external fragmentation but requires copying memory.

Segmentation divides a process’s address space into logical segments like code, heap, and stack, each with its own base and limit. Segments can be shared or grow independently but still suffer from external fragmentation.

Paging divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size, eliminating external fragmentation. A virtual address is split into a page number and offset, with the page table mapping pages to frames.

The translation lookaside buffer (TLB) caches recent address translations to speed up access, reducing the need for repeated memory lookups. TLB hit rates are typically above 99% due to locality of reference.

Multi-level page tables organize page tables hierarchically to reduce memory usage, especially in large address spaces. This approach creates only tables for used regions, but TLB misses become more costly.

documents.overview: Virtual memory uses demand paging to load program pages into memory only when needed, reducing memory usage and startup time. Page faults occur when a page is not in memory, causing delays due to disk access. The kernel must replace pages when memory is full, using algorithms like FIFO, LRU, or clock to minimize faults. Thrashing happens when too many processes compete for limited memory, causing system slowdowns. Memory-mapped files and swap space extend virtual memory to disk for file-backed and anonymous pages, respectively.

key_points.text: Virtual memory allows processes to use more memory than physically available by storing inactive pages on disk and loading them only when accessed (demand paging).
A page fault occurs when a process accesses a page not in memory, causing a delay of milliseconds due to disk access, which significantly slows down programs if frequent (cost of a page fault).
When no free memory frames are available, the kernel must evict a page to make space, writing dirty pages back to disk before replacement (page replacement).
The FIFO algorithm evicts the oldest page in memory but can cause Belady’s anomaly, where increasing frames worsens page faults for certain reference patterns.
The optimal (OPT) algorithm minimizes faults by replacing the page that won’t be used for the longest time, though it cannot be implemented in practice due to its reliance on future knowledge.
LRU (Least Recently Used) approximates OPT by replacing the page least recently accessed, avoiding Belady’s anomaly but requiring expensive tracking of access timestamps.

The clock algorithm approximates LRU by giving each page a ‘second chance’ if accessed recently, using a circular frame list and referenced bits to decide eviction, preferring clean pages to avoid disk writes.

documents.overview: A file system organizes storage into named files and directories, using metadata like inodes to track file attributes and data block locations. It manages block allocation through methods like contiguous, linked, or indexed allocation, while tracking free space with bitmaps or lists. The system balances block size for performance and efficiency, and provides mechanisms like hard and symbolic links for file references. The virtual file system layer allows multiple file system types to be accessed uniformly, while permissions control access to files and directories.

key_points.text: A file system organizes storage into named files and directories, which are accessed via paths starting from the root directory.
Each file is described by an inode, which stores metadata such as size, owner, permissions, timestamps, and data block locations, but not the file name.
Hard links are multiple directory entries pointing to the same inode, while symbolic links store a path to another file and can break if the target is moved or deleted.

Block allocation methods include contiguous allocation (fast but prone to fragmentation), linked allocation (flexible but prone to pointer damage), and indexed allocation (using pointers or extents for efficiency).
Free space is tracked using bitmaps or lists of free extents, helping maintain contiguous allocation and reduce fragmentation.
Block size impacts performance and efficiency, with larger blocks reducing overhead for large files but wasting space for small files; most systems use 4 kilobytes.
Opening a file involves path resolution, permission checks, and recording the current offset in an open-file table, with subsequent operations using a file descriptor.

documents.overview: The crash consistency problem arises when file system updates are interrupted by power loss, leaving data in an inconsistent state. Early solutions like fsck repaired inconsistencies after crashes but were slow and incomplete. Journaling and advanced file system designs like log-structured and copy-on-write systems improve reliability by ensuring updates are durable or atomic. Proper write ordering and caching strategies are critical to maintaining consistency across all layers.

key_points.text: File system operations often update multiple structures (e.g., data blocks, inodes, bitmaps) sequentially, risking partial updates on crash, which can corrupt data or cause space leaks.
Early Unix systems used fsck to detect and repair inconsistencies after crashes by rebuilding structures like inodes and bitmaps, but this process was slow and could not restore lost user data.

Journaling (write-ahead logging) writes a transaction record to a dedicated journal before applying changes to the main file system, ensuring durability and enabling fast recovery by replaying committed transactions.

Metadata journaling (ordered mode) only journals critical structures like inodes and bitmaps, reducing write overhead, but requires data blocks to be written before committing metadata to prevent dangling pointers.
Log-structured file systems store all data and metadata sequentially in a log, avoiding in-place updates but requiring a cleaner to reclaim dead blocks from old segments.
Copy-on-write systems like ZFS and Btrfs avoid overwrites by creating new copies of blocks and updating pointers atomically, enabling efficient snapshots by preserving old versions.
Writes must be forced to disk in a specific order (journal blocks before commit, commit before checkpointing) to prevent inconsistencies, often using cache flushes or flags like force-unit-access.

documents.overview: The document explains how hard disk drives (HDDs) and solid-state drives (SSDs) function, focusing on their mechanics, scheduling algorithms, and performance metrics. It also covers RAID configurations for improving storage reliability and speed, as well as key factors like write amplification and how to measure storage performance. Modern drives often handle scheduling internally, while SSDs rely on flash memory with unique write rules and wear-leveling techniques.

key_points.text: Hard disk drives store data magnetically on spinning platters divided into tracks and sectors, with read operations involving seek time, rotational latency, and data transfer. Seek and rotational latency dominate performance, making sequential reads much faster than random reads.

Disk scheduling algorithms like First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) and Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF) reorder requests to reduce head movement. FCFS is fair but inefficient, while SSTF minimizes seek distance but can starve requests at disk edges.

SCAN (elevator algorithm) and its variants (C-SCAN, LOOK, C-LOOK) move the disk arm in one direction, serving requests along the way. Modern drives often handle scheduling internally, and SSDs may bypass scheduling entirely due to their low-latency random access.

Solid-state drives use flash memory with no moving parts, making random and sequential reads similarly fast. Flash requires erasing entire blocks before rewriting, leading to wear leveling and garbage collection to extend drive lifespan.

Write amplification occurs in SSDs when one logical write triggers multiple physical writes during garbage collection, slowing performance and accelerating wear. Over-provisioning (extra spare capacity) mitigates this issue.

RAID configurations combine multiple drives for speed, reliability, or both. RAID 0 stripes data without redundancy, RAID 1 mirrors data for redundancy, and RAID 5/6 use parity for fault tolerance but have trade-offs in performance and capacity.

Storage performance is measured by throughput (bandwidth), IOPS (operations per second), and latency. These metrics depend on workloads, with sequential transfers prioritizing throughput and databases focusing on IOPS.

documents.overview: Operating systems separate user mode from kernel mode to protect the system, allowing only kernel mode to execute privileged operations like device access. System calls enable programs to request kernel services, while traps, exceptions, and interrupts manage transitions between modes and handle device events. Device drivers mediate between hardware and the kernel, using techniques like DMA and buffering to optimize data transfer. The kernel also implements blocking and non-blocking I/O to efficiently manage concurrent operations and device communication.

key_points.text: Processors operate in two modes: user mode, where programs run with restricted access, and kernel mode, where full privileges are granted. User mode prevents programs from executing privileged instructions, such as direct device access or interrupt manipulation, ensuring system stability by isolating crashes to individual programs.

System calls allow programs to request kernel services like file operations or process creation. A program invokes a system call by placing a system call number and arguments in predefined registers and executing a trap instruction, which switches the processor to kernel mode and triggers kernel handling. Libraries like the C library abstract system calls into higher-level functions, buffering small operations to reduce kernel crossings.

Traps, exceptions, and interrupts are mechanisms for handling events: traps are deliberate (e.g., system calls), exceptions occur due to errors (e.g., division by zero), and interrupts are asynchronous signals from devices (e.g., network packets or timers). Interrupts require brief handlers to avoid delaying further interrupts, often split into top and bottom halves for efficiency.

Polling and interrupts are two methods for detecting device completion. Polling involves continuous checking of device status, wasting CPU cycles but offering immediate response with no per-event overhead. Interrupts allow the CPU to handle other tasks until the device signals completion, but excessive interrupts can cause livelock, prompting adaptive techniques like switching between polling and interrupts under heavy load.

Direct Memory Access (DMA) enables devices to transfer large data blocks to memory without CPU intervention. The CPU configures a DMA controller with source, destination, and data size, allowing it to perform transfers independently and notify the CPU only upon completion. The kernel must ensure the memory pages involved in DMA transfers remain unmoved during the operation.

Device drivers are kernel modules responsible for communicating with hardware, translating hardware-specific operations into a uniform interface (e.g., block or character devices). They account for a significant portion of an OS’s codebase and are a major source of crashes due to their privileged execution.

The kernel manages data transfer between programs and devices through buffering, caching, and spooling. Buffering accommodates speed mismatches (e.g., fast programs and slow modems), caching stores frequently accessed data (e.g., disk blocks) for quicker retrieval, and spooling queues output for devices with limited capacity (e.g., printers) to prevent program delays.

calibration.point: Hard disk drives store data magnetically on spinning platters divided into tracks and sectors, with read operations involving seek time, rotational latency, and data transfer. Seek and rotational latency dominate performance, making sequential reads much faster than random reads.
calibration.passage_text:
Storage Devices and Disk Scheduling

Hard disk drives

A hard disk drive stores data magnetically on spinning platters. Each surface is divided into concentric tracks, and each track into sectors, traditionally of 512 bytes and now usually 4 kilobytes. A set of read-write heads on a single arm moves across the surfaces. Reading a sector takes three steps: the arm moves to the right track, the seek; the drive waits for the sector to rotate under the head, the rotational latency; and the data passes under the head, the transfer.

Seek and rotation dominate. An average seek takes several milliseconds, and at 7,200 revolutions per minute one rotation takes about 8.3 milliseconds, so the average rotational latency is about 4 milliseconds. Transferring 4 kilobytes, by contrast, takes a few tens of microseconds. The consequence is that a disk reading sequentially can deliver over 100 megabytes per second, while the same disk reading small blocks at random positions may manage only about a hundred operations per second.

calibration.point: Prevention strategies break one of the four conditions, such as enforcing a global lock order to prevent circular wait or requiring all resources to be requested at once.
calibration.passage_text:
Prevention

Deadlock prevention designs the system so that one of the four conditions can never hold.

Mutual exclusion usually cannot be removed, since some resources are inherently unshareable. Hold and wait can be removed by requiring a thread to request all its resources at once, before it starts, which wastes resources that sit allocated but unused and can starve threads that need many popular resources. No preemption can be removed for resources whose state is easy to save and restore, such as CPU registers

or memory, but not for a lock in the middle of an update.

The most practical prevention rule breaks circular wait: give every lock a number and require that threads always acquire locks in increasing order. A cycle would then need some thread to wait for a lower-numbered lock while holding a higher one, which the rule forbids. Large programs such as operating system kernels document a global lock order for exactly this reason, and tools exist that check the order at run time.

calibration.point: Block allocation methods include contiguous allocation (fast but prone to fragmentation), linked allocation (flexible but prone to pointer damage), and indexed allocation (using pointers or extents for efficiency).
calibration.passage_text: Indexed allocation gives each file an index of its block addresses. The classic Unix inode holds twelve direct pointers to data blocks, then a single indirect pointer to a block full of further pointers, a double indirect pointer, and a triple indirect pointer. Small files, which are the majority, are reached with no extra reads at all, while very large files remain possible. Modern file systems such as ext4 replace long lists of pointers with extents: an extent records a starting block and a length, so one entry can describe a run of thousands of contiguous blocks.

calibration.point: Round robin assigns fixed time quanta to processes, improving response time for interactive work but requiring careful quantum selection to avoid excessive context switching.
calibration.passage_text:
Round robin

Round robin gives each ready process a fixed time quantum, typically between 10 and 100 milliseconds, in turn. When the quantum expires the process is preempted and placed at the tail of the ready queue. No process waits more than (n minus 1) quanta before its next turn, which gives good response time for interactive work.

The choice of quantum matters. If the quantum is very large, round robin behaves like first-come, first-served. If it is very small, the CPU spends a large share of its time on context switches instead of useful work. A common rule of thumb is to choose a quantum longer than most CPU bursts, so that most processes block for I/O before their quantum runs out.

calibration.point: The kernel manages data transfer between programs and devices through buffering, caching, and spooling. Buffering accommodates speed mismatches (e.g., fast programs and slow modems), caching stores frequently accessed data (e.g., disk blocks) for quicker retrieval, and spooling queues output for devices with limited capacity (e.g., printers) to prevent program delays.
calibration.passage_text:
Device drivers

A device driver is the kernel code that knows how to operate one kind of device: which registers to write, how to start a transfer and what each interrupt means. Drivers present a uniform interface to the rest of the kernel, typically as block devices that read and write fixed-size blocks, such as disks, or as character devices that produce or consume streams of bytes, such as keyboards and serial ports. Drivers make up most of an operating system's source code and are responsible for a large share of its crashes, since they run in kernel mode with full privileges.

calibration.point: Priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes, so aging gradually increases priorities over time to ensure fairness.
calibration.passage_text:
Priority scheduling and aging

Priority scheduling runs the highest-priority ready process. Priorities can be set externally, for example by an administrator, or computed internally from measurable quantities such as memory needs or the ratio of I/O to computation. Shortest job first is a special case in which the priority is the predicted burst length.

A low-priority process can starve when higher-priority work never stops arriving. The standard remedy is aging: the scheduler gradually raises the priority of a process the longer it waits, so that eventually even the lowest-priority process runs. A story told about an old IBM mainframe holds that when it was shut down, a low-priority job submitted years earlier was found still waiting.

calibration.point: Direct Memory Access (DMA) enables devices to transfer large data blocks to memory without CPU intervention. The CPU configures a DMA controller with source, destination, and data size, allowing it to perform transfers independently and notify the CPU only upon completion. The kernel must ensure the memory pages involved in DMA transfers remain unmoved during the operation.
calibration.passage_text:
Polling versus interrupts

There are two ways for the CPU to learn that a device has finished. With polling, also called busy waiting, the CPU repeatedly reads the device's status register until the ready bit appears. Polling wastes the CPU while it waits, but it reacts with no delay and has no per-event overhead. With interrupts, the CPU does other work and the device signals when it is done. Interrupts are better for slow devices, but each one costs a context save and a handler. A very fast network card can produce so many interrupts that the CPU does nothing but handle them, a condition called receive livelock. Modern network drivers therefore switch adaptively: they use interrupts when traffic is light and fall back to polling under heavy load.

calibration.point: First-come, first-served scheduling runs processes in arrival order but can cause long waits for short jobs due to the convoy effect, leaving I/O devices idle.
calibration.passage_text:
First-come, first-served

First-come, first-served runs processes in the order they arrive and never preempts them. It is fair in a narrow sense and trivial to implement with a queue, but its average waiting time can be poor. When one long CPU-bound job arrives just ahead of many short ones, every short job waits for the long one to finish. This pile-up of short processes stuck behind a long one is called the convoy effect, and it also leaves the I/O devices idle while the short jobs wait for their turn.

calibration.point: Avoidance, like Dijkstra’s banker’s algorithm, grants requests only if the system remains in a safe state where all threads can eventually finish.
calibration.passage_text:
Avoidance and the banker's algorithm

Deadlock avoidance allows all four conditions in principle but examines every request and grants it only if the system stays in a safe state. A state is safe if there is some order in which every thread can obtain its maximum remaining needs and finish. An unsafe state is not yet a deadlock, but it may lead to one.

Dijkstra's banker's algorithm implements avoidance. Each thread declares in advance the maximum number of each resource it may ever need. When a request arrives, the algorithm pretends to grant it and then searches for a safe sequence: repeatedly find a thread whose remaining need fits within the currently available resources, assume it finishes and returns everything it holds, and continue. If every thread can finish this way, the request is granted; otherwise the requesting thread waits. The algorithm is named after a banker who never lends out cash in a way that would leave him unable to satisfy all his customers' credit limits. Its weakness is practical: few programs know their maximum needs in advance, and the number of threads changes all the time.

calibration.point: Device drivers are kernel modules responsible for communicating with hardware, translating hardware-specific operations into a uniform interface (e.g., block or character devices). They account for a significant portion of an OS’s codebase and are a major source of crashes due to their privileged execution.
calibration.passage_text:
Direct memory access

Copying a large block of data from a device to memory one word at a time would keep the CPU busy throughout. With direct memory access, or DMA, the CPU instead tells a DMA controller the source, the destination in memory, and the number of bytes, and then goes on with other work. The controller moves the data by itself and raises a single interrupt when the transfer is complete. Disks, network cards and graphics cards all use DMA for bulk transfers. Because the controller writes to physical memory directly, the kernel must make sure the pages involved are not evicted or moved during the transfer.

calibration.point: The optimal (OPT) algorithm minimizes faults by replacing the page that won’t be used for the longest time, though it cannot be implemented in practice due to its reliance on future knowledge.
calibration.passage_text:
The optimal algorithm

The optimal policy, sometimes called OPT or MIN, evicts the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future. It provably produces the fewest possible faults for any reference string. It cannot be implemented in a real system, because the kernel cannot see the future, but it is valuable as a yardstick: in a simulation, a practical algorithm can be judged by how close it comes to the optimal fault count.

calibration.point: Race conditions occur when threads share data and the outcome depends on the timing of their operations, such as lost increments in a shared counter.
calibration.passage_text:
Synchronization

Race conditions

When threads share data, the result of their work can depend on the exact interleaving of their instructions. Consider two threads that each add one to a shared counter. The statement looks atomic, but the machine performs three steps: load the counter into a register, add one, and store it back. If both threads load the old value before either stores, both store the same result and one increment is lost. A bug like this, whose outcome depends on timing, is called a race condition. It may appear once in a million runs, which makes it painful to reproduce.

calibration.point: Polling and interrupts are two methods for detecting device completion. Polling involves continuous checking of device status, wasting CPU cycles but offering immediate response with no per-event overhead. Interrupts allow the CPU to handle other tasks until the device signals completion, but excessive interrupts can cause livelock, prompting adaptive techniques like switching between polling and interrupts under heavy load.
calibration.passage_text:
Traps, exceptions and interrupts

The processor stops normal execution for three kinds of reasons. A trap is deliberate, caused by an instruction such as the system call instruction. An exception is caused by the current instruction going wrong, such as a division by zero or a page fault. Both are synchronous: they happen at a specific instruction of the running program. An interrupt, in contrast, is asynchronous: it is raised by a device, such as a network card announcing that a packet has arrived or a timer announcing that a time slice has ended, and it arrives regardless of what the processor is executing.

On an interrupt, the processor saves the current program counter and status, switches to kernel mode, and jumps through the interrupt vector, a table of handler addresses indexed by interrupt number. The handler must be brief, because further interrupts may be delayed while it runs. Kernels therefore split interrupt handling in two: a top half acknowledges the device and records what happened, and a bottom half, run later with interrupts enabled, does the slower processing.

calibration.point: Write amplification occurs in SSDs when one logical write triggers multiple physical writes during garbage collection, slowing performance and accelerating wear. Over-provisioning (extra spare capacity) mitigates this issue.
calibration.passage_text:
Solid-state drives

A solid-state drive stores data in flash memory and has no moving parts, so a random read costs about the same as a sequential one, typically tens of microseconds. Flash has awkward rules, however. Data is written in pages of a few kilobytes, but a page cannot be overwritten in place: it must first be erased, and erasure works only on whole blocks of hundreds of pages. Each block also tolerates a limited number of erase cycles before it wears out.

The drive hides these rules behind a flash translation layer, firmware that maps logical block addresses to physical flash pages. Each write goes to a fresh, already erased page, and the old page is marked invalid. Garbage collection later copies the valid pages out of a block and erases it. Wear leveling spreads erasures evenly across all blocks so that no block wears out early. The TRIM command lets the operating system tell the drive which logical blocks no longer hold useful data, so garbage collection need not copy them.

calibration.point: System calls allow programs to request kernel services like file operations or process creation. A program invokes a system call by placing a system call number and arguments in predefined registers and executing a trap instruction, which switches the processor to kernel mode and triggers kernel handling. Libraries like the C library abstract system calls into higher-level functions, buffering small operations to reduce kernel crossings.
calibration.passage_text:
I/O, Interrupts and System Calls

User mode and kernel mode

Processors run in at least two privilege levels. In user mode, a program can execute ordinary instructions and access its own memory, but privileged instructions are forbidden: it cannot talk to devices directly, change page tables, or disable interrupts. In kernel mode everything is allowed. A mode bit in the processor records the current level. If a user program attempts a privileged instruction, the hardware raises an exception and the kernel takes over, usually ending the program. This separation is what lets one buggy program crash without taking the whole machine down.

calibration.point: Copy-on-write systems like ZFS and Btrfs avoid overwrites by creating new copies of blocks and updating pointers atomically, enabling efficient snapshots by preserving old versions.
calibration.passage_text:
Copy-on-write file systems

Copy-on-write file systems such as ZFS and Btrfs never overwrite a live block either. To change a block, they write a new copy elsewhere, then write a new copy of the block that points to it, and so on up the tree to the root. The final step atomically switches the single root pointer to the new tree. A crash before that switch leaves the old tree intact and consistent; a crash after it leaves the new tree. Because old trees remain valid until their blocks are reused, these file systems can keep snapshots of the whole file system almost for free.

calibration.point: A process is an active program in execution with its own memory and state, including separate text, data, heap, and stack segments.
calibration.passage_text:
Processes and Threads

What a process is

A program is a passive file on disk: a sequence of instructions and some initial data. A process is a program in execution, an active entity with its own state. When you start a text editor twice, there is one program but two processes, each with its own memory and its own idea of which file is open. The operating system creates processes, schedules them onto the CPU, gives them memory, and cleans up after them when they finish.

Each process has an address space laid out in regions. The text segment holds the machine code and is usually marked read-only. The data segment holds global and static variables. The heap grows upward as the program asks for memory at run time, and the stack grows downward as functions are called, holding local variables and return addresses. The gap between heap and stack lets both grow without colliding in the common case.

calibration.point: Disk scheduling algorithms like First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) and Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF) reorder requests to reduce head movement. FCFS is fair but inefficient, while SSTF minimizes seek distance but can starve requests at disk edges.
calibration.passage_text:
Storage Devices and Disk Scheduling

Hard disk drives

A hard disk drive stores data magnetically on spinning platters. Each surface is divided into concentric tracks, and each track into sectors, traditionally of 512 bytes and now usually 4 kilobytes. A set of read-write heads on a single arm moves across the surfaces. Reading a sector takes three steps: the arm moves to the right track, the seek; the drive waits for the sector to rotate under the head, the rotational latency; and the data passes under the head, the transfer.

Seek and rotation dominate. An average seek takes several milliseconds, and at 7,200 revolutions per minute one rotation takes about 8.3 milliseconds, so the average rotational latency is about 4 milliseconds. Transferring 4 kilobytes, by contrast, takes a few tens of microseconds. The consequence is that a disk reading sequentially can deliver over 100 megabytes per second, while the same disk reading small blocks at random positions may manage only about a hundred operations per second.

calibration.point: Hardware provides atomic instructions like test-and-set and compare-and-swap to safely implement locks without relying on program-order guarantees.
calibration.passage_text:
Atomic hardware instructions

Processors offer instructions that read and modify a memory location as one indivisible step. Test-and-set writes true to a location and returns its old value. Compare-and-swap writes a new value only if the location still holds an expected old value, and reports whether it succeeded. With either instruction a thread can claim a free lock in one step, because no other thread can slip in between the check and the update.

calibration.point: SCAN (elevator algorithm) and its variants (C-SCAN, LOOK, C-LOOK) move the disk arm in one direction, serving requests along the way. Modern drives often handle scheduling internally, and SSDs may bypass scheduling entirely due to their low-latency random access.
calibration.passage_text:
SCAN, known as the elevator algorithm, moves the arm steadily in one direction, serving every request it passes, until it reaches the end of the disk, then reverses. No request waits for more than two sweeps. Its variant C-SCAN serves requests in one direction only and then returns the arm to the start without serving anything on the way back, which gives more uniform waiting times, because a request just behind the head no longer waits for a full return sweep of the other direction first. LOOK and C-LOOK behave like SCAN and C-SCAN but turn around at the last pending request instead of travelling all the way to the edge.

Modern drives accept many requests at once and reorder them internally, because only the drive knows its exact geometry and the rotational position of the platters. Linux on solid-state drives often uses no scheduler at all, simply passing requests through in order.

calibration.point: Threads are lightweight execution units within a process that share memory but have their own stack and registers, enabling parallelism and responsiveness.
calibration.passage_text: responding to its user in one thread while another waits for the network.

calibration.point: A page fault occurs when a process accesses a page not in memory, causing a delay of milliseconds due to disk access, which significantly slows down programs if frequent (cost of a page fault).
calibration.passage_text:
Virtual Memory and Page Replacement

Demand paging

Virtual memory lets a process use more memory than is physically present by keeping only part of its address space in RAM and the rest on disk. With demand paging, a page is loaded only when the process first touches it. A program that never uses its error-handling code never pays to load it, and a process can start running before all of its executable has been read.

Pages not in memory are marked invalid in the page table. When the process touches one, the hardware raises a page fault and the kernel takes over. It checks that the address is legal at all, finds a free frame, schedules a disk read to bring the page in, and blocks the process meanwhile. When the read completes, the kernel updates the page table entry to valid and restarts the faulting instruction, which now succeeds. If the address was not legal, the kernel instead sends the process a segmentation fault signal.

calibration.point: Paging divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size, eliminating external fragmentation. A virtual address is split into a page number and offset, with the page table mapping pages to frames.
calibration.passage_text:
Paging

Paging divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size, commonly 4 kilobytes. Any page can be placed in any free frame, so a process's memory no longer needs to be contiguous and external fragmentation disappears. A virtual address is split into a page number and an offset within the page. The memory management unit looks the page number up in the process's page table, which gives the frame number, and appends the unchanged offset to form the physical address.

Each page table entry holds the frame number plus several bits: a valid bit saying whether the page is mapped at all, protection bits for read, write and execute, a dirty bit set by the hardware when the page is written, and a referenced bit set when it is accessed. The kernel uses the dirty and referenced bits when it decides which pages to evict.

calibration.point: Log-structured file systems store all data and metadata sequentially in a log, avoiding in-place updates but requiring a cleaner to reclaim dead blocks from old segments.
calibration.passage_text:
Log-structured file systems

A log-structured file system takes the journal idea to its conclusion: the log is the only place data lives. All writes, data and metadata alike, are buffered in memory and written sequentially to the end of the log in large segments, never overwriting anything in place. Sequential writes are fast on hard disks, which made this design attractive when memory caches began to absorb most reads. Because the newest version of each inode keeps moving, a small inode map records where the current copy of each inode is. The cost is cleaning: old segments fill with dead blocks that later writes have superseded, and a cleaner must copy the live blocks out of partly empty segments so that whole segments can be reused.

calibration.point: File system operations often update multiple structures (e.g., data blocks, inodes, bitmaps) sequentially, risking partial updates on crash, which can corrupt data or cause space leaks.
calibration.passage_text:
Crash Consistency and Journaling

The crash consistency problem

Many file system operations update several structures on the device. Appending one block to a file, for instance, must write the new data block, update the file's inode with the new size and block pointer, and mark the block as used in the free-space bitmap. The device writes these blocks one at a time, and power can fail between any two of them. If only the bitmap update reaches the disk, a block is marked used but belongs to no file, a space leak. If only the inode update reaches the disk, the inode points to a block that still holds garbage, and the bitmap may later hand that same block to another file. The file system must survive such partial updates without losing its structure.

calibration.point: The operating system maintains a process control block for each process, storing details like registers, program counter, scheduling info, memory mappings, open files, and CPU usage.
calibration.passage_text:
The process control block

The kernel keeps one record per process, called the process control block. It stores everything needed to stop the process and resume it later as if nothing had happened: the saved program counter and registers, the process identifier, the current state, scheduling information such as priority, a pointer to the page tables that describe its memory, the list of open files, and accounting data such as CPU time used so far. On Linux this record is the task_struct, and the kernel links all of them into lists that the scheduler walks.

calibration.point: Solid-state drives use flash memory with no moving parts, making random and sequential reads similarly fast. Flash requires erasing entire blocks before rewriting, leading to wear leveling and garbage collection to extend drive lifespan.
calibration.passage_text:
Solid-state drives

A solid-state drive stores data in flash memory and has no moving parts, so a random read costs about the same as a sequential one, typically tens of microseconds. Flash has awkward rules, however. Data is written in pages of a few kilobytes, but a page cannot be overwritten in place: it must first be erased, and erasure works only on whole blocks of hundreds of pages. Each block also tolerates a limited number of erase cycles before it wears out.

The drive hides these rules behind a flash translation layer, firmware that maps logical block addresses to physical flash pages. Each write goes to a fresh, already erased page, and the old page is marked invalid. Garbage collection later copies the valid pages out of a block and erases it. Wear leveling spreads erasures evenly across all blocks so that no block wears out early. The TRIM command lets the operating system tell the drive which logical blocks no longer hold useful data, so garbage collection need not copy them.

calibration.point: External fragmentation occurs when free memory becomes scattered into small holes due to variable-sized allocations, while internal fragmentation wastes space inside fixed-size allocations. Compaction can reduce external fragmentation but requires copying memory.
calibration.passage_text:
Fragmentation

Allocating variable-sized contiguous blocks leads to external fragmentation: over time free memory becomes scattered into many small holes between allocated blocks, so a request may fail even though the total free memory would be enough. Allocation policies such as first fit, best fit and worst fit choose which hole to use, but none avoids the problem. Compaction moves allocated blocks together to merge the holes, at the price of copying memory.

The opposite problem is internal fragmentation: space wasted inside an allocated block because the block is larger than what was requested. If memory is handed out only in fixed units of 4 kilobytes, a request for 4,097 bytes receives two units and wastes almost a whole one. Fixed-size allocation removes external fragmentation entirely but always pays some internal fragmentation in the last unit of each allocation.

calibration.point: Four conditions must hold simultaneously for a deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Removing any one prevents deadlock.
calibration.passage_text:
The four necessary conditions

Edward Coffman and colleagues showed in 1971 that a deadlock can arise only if four conditions hold at the same time:

•  Mutual exclusion: at least one resource can be held by only one thread at a time.

•  Hold and wait: a thread holds at least one resource while waiting to acquire more.

•  No preemption: a resource cannot be taken away from the thread holding it; it is only released voluntarily.

•  Circular wait: there is a cycle of threads, each waiting for a resource held by the next one in the cycle.

Because all four are necessary, removing any one of them makes deadlock impossible. Every strategy for handling deadlock works by breaking one of these conditions, by steering around unsafe situations, or by detecting deadlock after it happens.

calibration.point: Traps, exceptions, and interrupts are mechanisms for handling events: traps are deliberate (e.g., system calls), exceptions occur due to errors (e.g., division by zero), and interrupts are asynchronous signals from devices (e.g., network packets or timers). Interrupts require brief handlers to avoid delaying further interrupts, often split into top and bottom halves for efficiency.
calibration.passage_text:
System calls

A program that needs a service only the kernel can provide, such as reading a file or creating a process, makes a system call. The program places a system call number and its arguments in agreed registers and executes a special trap instruction, such as syscall on x86-64. The trap switches the processor to kernel mode and jumps to a fixed entry point that the kernel installed at boot, so a program cannot jump into arbitrary kernel code. The kernel looks the number up in its system call table, checks every argument, since a pointer passed from user space might point anywhere, performs the work, places a return value in a register, and returns to user mode.

Most programmers never execute the trap instruction themselves. The C library wraps each system call in an ordinary function, such as read or write, which sets up the registers and handles the error convention: on failure the function returns minus one and stores an error code in errno. Because each crossing into the kernel costs hundreds of nanoseconds or more, libraries buffer small operations; the printf function, for example, collects output in memory and makes one write call for many lines.
